intent: Prefer the simplest design that fully satisfies the requirement, and treat every unnecessary indirection, configuration knob and speculative branch as a defect with a carrying cost.
problem: Complexity added without a requirement behind it — a framework for one call site, a plugin registry with no plugins, a generic abstraction over two concrete cases — pays for itself forever in reading, testing and debugging, while delivering no value now.
context: Applies when the solution to be built is well understood and stable enough that the shape of the answer is known. 'Stupid' in the original refers to the repairer: the design must be understandable by an average maintainer with basic tools, not just its author. KISS is a tie-breaker between designs of equal adequacy, not a licence to under-engineer — it is violated by a simple design that fails the requirement just as much as by a clever one that does.
benefits: Lower cognitive load: fewer moving parts to hold in mind while debugging.
Faster onboarding — a new maintainer can hold the whole design in working memory.
Fewer places to test, and each test covers more of what actually ships.
Less to change later; simplification is the cheapest form of maintenance.
Failure modes stay local and diagnosable because there are fewer interacting mechanisms.
tradeoffs: Simplicity has a carrying cost, not a zero cost: 'simplest that works' still has to be found, and finding it takes design effort.
Applying KISS to unfamiliar or volatile requirements produces a design that must be rewritten; the cost is deferred, not avoided.
Observed as "we could always add it later", it becomes an excuse for under-delivering required functionality.
Reduces forward-looking flexibility — legitimate cases (multi-tenancy, compliance) exist where the expensive design is the correct one today.
The principle is qualitative: two competent engineers can honestly disagree about which design is simpler.
quality_attributes_note: simplicity 10 by definition; extensibility 4 is the deliberate trade-off. security 5 because simplicity helps auditability but KISS says nothing about threat modelling.

participants.responsibility: Defines what must actually be satisfied; the boundary for what counts as unnecessary complexity.
participants.notes: Anything traceable to a stated requirement is not speculative.

participants.responsibility: The hypothetical average engineer who must repair the design later.
participants.notes: Kelly Johnson framed the principle around field repair under combat conditions.

use_cases: Replacing a four-class strategy hierarchy covering two real cases with a switch or two implementations.
Dropping a plugin registry in favour of direct construction when there is exactly one plugin.
Not building a general-purpose workflow engine for a three-step approval.
Choosing a simple polling loop over an event-driven pipeline for a low-volume batch job.
Using a standard library container instead of a custom collection.
avoid_when: The requirement is genuinely volatile and the cost of redesign is high (e.g. a payment protocol, a storage format others depend on).
The complexity is load-bearing: security, concurrency correctness or regulatory compliance is not optional.
A platform constraint forces it — you cannot make a driver simpler than the hardware it drives.
The "simple" version is only simple because it defers the hard part to an unmaintainable workaround.
You are removing complexity that exists to absorb real, observed change, not imagined change.
pitfalls: Using 'simplest' to justify omitting error handling, input validation or tests.
Oversimplifying the problem statement first, then implementing it perfectly.
Clever code that is shorter than the obvious version but requires the reader to hold more state.
Collapsing two genuinely different rules into one flag parameter to reduce line count.
Applying KISS to the domain model rather than the infrastructure — the domain is where complexity is legitimate.

related_patterns_notes.yagni-principle: YAGNI decides *whether* to build a capability; KISS decides *how simply* to build it once the requirement exists.
related_patterns_notes.rule-of-three: Rule of Three is KISS applied specifically to abstraction: do not build the general mechanism before the third concrete case.

anti_patterns: A framework in an application, built before the application exists.
Configuration flags for behaviour that has exactly one value in the deployment.
Premature generalisation into generics, base classes or plugin points with one implementation.
Meta-programming to avoid four lines of straightforward code.
Using "simple" as an argument against a requirement that was actually asked for.
design_principles: Most systems work best when kept simple rather than made complicated; simplicity should be a design goal (U.S. Navy, 1960).
Design for the average maintainer with basic tools, not for the designer's cleverness (Kelly Johnson).
Perfection is attained not when there is nothing more to add, but when there is nothing left to take away (de Saint-Exupéry, as cited on the KISS page).
best_practices: Apply KISS as a tie-breaker among designs that all satisfy the requirement.
Prefer the platform/stdlib mechanism over a bespoke one unless a measured requirement says otherwise.
Review proposals by asking "which requirement forces this piece of complexity?"
Keep the complex part in one well-named place so the rest stays simple.
sources: Ben R. Rich, Clarence Leonard (Kelly) Johnson 1910-1990: A Biographical Memoir, National Academies Press 1995, p. 13 (origin of the phrase)
